lessons.title: Classification of Rice Varieties
lessons.body: Rice is broadly classified into two species: Oryza sativa (Asian rice) and Oryza glaberrima (African rice). In Africa, O. glaberrima is native to West Africa and is known for its hardiness, but it shatters easily and has lower yield. Most commercial rice in Africa is O. sativa, which includes indica and japonica types. Indica rices are long, slender grains that cook fluffy and separate; they are grown in the lowland tropics and are the most common in Africa. Japonica rices are short, round grains that cook sticky; they are grown in temperate regions and high-altitude areas like Ethiopia and Madagascar. A third group, javanica, is intermediate. You can also classify by ecology: lowland (paddy) rice grows in flooded fields; upland rice grows on dry land, often in rotation with other crops. Lowland rice yields more but needs water control. Upland rice yields less but is important for food security in hilly areas. Another classification is by grain length: long (over 6.6 mm), medium (5.5â6.6 mm), and short (less than 5.5 mm). Grain length affects milling: long grains break more easily. Also, glutinous (waxy) rice is sticky when cooked and is used for special foods. Aromatic rices like Basmati and Jasmine are long-grain and prized for smell. In Africa, local varieties like Nerica (New Rice for Africa) combine African and Asian traits for drought tolerance and higher yield. Knowing these classes helps you set your mill correctly: long-grain rice needs gentler handling to reduce breakage.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Paddy
lessons.body: Paddy is rice still in its husk. Its physical properties determine how you mill it. Key properties include grain dimensions (length, width, thickness), weight (1000-grain weight), hardness, moisture content, and husk content. Length ranges from 5 to 10 mm, width from 2 to 4 mm. A typical 1000-grain weight is 20â30 grams. Hardness affects breakage: harder grains resist cracking. Moisture content is critical: ideal for milling is 12â14%. Too dry (below 12%) makes grains brittle and they shatter; too wet (above 14%) makes them sticky and clog the mill. You can test moisture with a simple moisture meter or by biting a grainâif it shatters, it's too dry; if it chews, it's too wet. Husk content is about 20% of paddy weight. After milling, you get about 60â65% white rice, 20% husk, 10% bran, and 5% germ and losses. Grain shape matters: long slender grains break more easily than short round ones. Also, chalkiness (white opaque spots) weakens grains and lowers milling yield. You can check chalkiness by holding grains against light. Foreign matter like stones, straw, and dirt should be removed before milling to prevent damage. In Africa, many farmers thresh by hand, leaving more foreign matter, so cleaning is essential. Use a simple screen or winnowing to remove light matter. Proper storage keeps moisture stable; store paddy in dry, ventilated bags off the floor. These physical properties guide your mill settings: adjust roller clearance based on grain size, and set husker speed to avoid cracking.

lessons.title: Chemical Composition of Rice Kernels
lessons.body: A rice kernel is mostly starch (about 75â80% of dry weight), with protein (7â8%), fat (2â3%), and small amounts of fibre, vitamins, and minerals. Starch is the main energy source. It comes in two forms: amylose and amylopectin. Amylose makes rice firm and separate; amylopectin makes it sticky. Long-grain indica rices have high amylose (22â30%), while short-grain japonica have low amylose (0â20%). This affects cooking and milling: high-amylose rice tends to break more during milling because it is less flexible. Protein content is higher in the bran and germ, so white rice has less protein than brown rice. Fat is mostly in the bran and germ; it can go rancid if stored too long, so bran should be removed quickly. Vitamins and minerals (B vitamins, iron, zinc) are concentrated in the bran and germ. Milling removes these, which is why white rice is less nutritious. In Africa, where rice is a staple, this matters for nutrition. You can reduce nutrient loss by milling less (e.g., brown rice) or by fortifying white rice. The chemical composition also affects milling: high-fat rice can clog rollers if not cleaned. High-moisture rice has more free water, making it softer and harder to mill without breakage. To test composition simply, you can't do lab tests, but you can observe: rice with a lot of bran (darker) has more nutrients. Aromatic rice has volatile compounds (like 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline) that give smell. These compounds are lost during milling if you over-polish. So, for aromatic varieties, mill gently and avoid excessive polishing.

lessons.title: Differences Between Indica and Japonica Rice
lessons.body: Indica and japonica are the two major subspecies of Asian rice. Indica rices are grown in tropical and subtropical lowlands, including most of Africa. They have long, slender grains, and when cooked, they are fluffy and separate. Japonica rices are grown in temperate regions and high altitudes, like Ethiopia and Madagascar. They have short, round grains and cook sticky and moist. Indica plants are usually taller, tiller more, and are less resistant to cold. Japonica plants are shorter, have fewer tillers, and tolerate cold better. In milling, indica grains are longer and more prone to breaking because they are slender. Japonica grains are shorter and rounder, so they break less. Indica rice usually has higher amylose, making it firmer; japonica has lower amylose, making it stickier. This affects milling: indica may need slower roller speeds to reduce breakage. Japonica may need less polishing because it is already sticky. In Africa, indica is dominant because it suits the climate. However, Nerica varieties are interspecific crosses between African rice (O. glaberrima) and Asian rice (O. sativa), often with indica traits. They combine drought tolerance with higher yield. When you mill, check the grain type: if it's long and slender, treat it as indica; if short and round, treat it as japonica. Adjust husker clearance: indica needs wider clearance to avoid cracking; japonica can take tighter clearance. Also, cooking quality differs: consumers in West Africa prefer long-grain indica for dishes like jollof rice, while some East African markets prefer japonica for sticky dishes. Know your market to choose varieties and milling settings.

lessons.title: Impact of Variety on Milling Yield
lessons.body: Milling yield is the amount of white rice you get from paddy. It varies by variety. Typically, you get 60â65% head rice (whole grains) and 5â10% broken grains, plus bran and husk. But some varieties give higher yields. For example, long-grain indica rices often have lower head rice yield because they break more easily. Short-grain japonica rices tend to have higher head rice yield because they are rounder and stronger. Nerica varieties can give good yields if milled properly. Other factors: grain hardness, chalkiness, and moisture content. Hard, translucent grains mill better than soft, chalky ones. Chalky grains break easily. Moisture content: if too dry, grains shatter; if too wet, they mash. So, adjust moisture to 12â14% before milling. Also, the milling process itself: a two-step process (husking then polishing) gives higher yield than a one-step. In Africa, many small mills use single-pass machines, which cause more breakage. You can improve yield by using a rubber-roll husker instead of a steel husker, and by setting the roller clearance correctly. For long-grain rice, use a clearance of about 0.5â0.8 mm; for short-grain, 0.3â0.5 mm. Also, screen the paddy to remove immature grains, which break easily. Immature grains are lighter and can be removed by winnowing. By choosing the right variety and milling carefully, you can increase head rice yield by 5â10%. That means more income. For example, if you mill 100 kg of paddy, a good yield gives 60 kg head rice; a poor yield gives 50 kg. At $1 per kg, that's $10 difference. So, variety matters.

lessons.title: Grain Grading and Specifications
lessons.body: Grain grading sorts milled rice by quality. It affects price. Grades are based on head rice percentage, broken rice percentage, foreign matter, discoloration, and moisture. In many African markets, grades are: Grade 1 (premium): at least 95% head rice, no foreign matter, no discolored grains. Grade 2: 80â94% head rice, minimal foreign matter. Grade 3: 60â79% head rice, some broken and foreign matter. Below that is off-grade. To grade, you need simple tools: a sieve to separate broken from head rice, a scale to weigh, and your eyes. Take a 100-gram sample. Remove foreign matter (stones, straw). Weigh the head rice (grains at least 75% of original length). Calculate percentage. For example, if you have 85 grams head rice, that's 85%. Also check discoloration: yellow or black grains lower grade. Moisture should be 12â14%; test with a moisture meter or by feel. In Africa, many millers sell to local traders who set their own standards. But for export or formal markets, you need to meet standards like those of the West African Rice Development Association (WARDA) or international ISO. For example, Grade 1 rice must have less than 0.1% foreign matter. To improve grade, you can use a destoner to remove stones, a paddy separator to remove immature grains, and a color sorter (if available) to remove discolored grains. Even without machines, you can hand-pick. Grading also involves labeling: put rice in clean bags, label with grade, weight, and date. This builds trust and gets better prices. Remember: consistent grading leads to repeat customers.

quiz.q: Which species of rice is native to Africa?
quiz.explanation: Oryza glaberrima is the African rice species, known for hardiness but lower yield.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for milling paddy?
quiz.explanation: 12â14% moisture prevents breakage and clogging during milling.

quiz.q: Which type of rice is typically long-grain and cooks fluffy?
quiz.explanation: Indica rice has long, slender grains and high amylose, making it fluffy when cooked.

quiz.q: What percentage of paddy weight is husk?
quiz.explanation: Husk makes up about 20% of paddy weight and is removed during milling.

quiz.q: Which chemical component makes rice sticky?
quiz.explanation: Amylopectin is a branched starch that causes stickiness, while amylose makes rice firm.

quiz.q: What is a key difference between indica and japonica rice plants?
quiz.explanation: Japonica rice is more cold-tolerant and is grown in temperate and high-altitude regions.

quiz.q: Which factor does NOT affect milling yield?
quiz.explanation: Bag color is irrelevant to milling yield; hardness, moisture, and chalkiness are key factors.

quiz.q: What is the minimum head rice percentage for Grade 1 rice in many African markets?
quiz.explanation: Grade 1 premium rice typically requires at least 95% head rice.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to separate broken rice from head rice?
quiz.explanation: A sieve with appropriate mesh size separates broken grains from whole head rice.

quiz.q: What is Nerica?
options: B) A rice variety combining African and Asian traits
quiz.explanation: Nerica (New Rice for Africa) is an interspecific cross with drought tolerance and higher yield.

quiz.q: Which grain shape is more prone to breakage during milling?
quiz.explanation: Long slender grains are more fragile and break more easily than short round grains.

quiz.q: What is the typical protein content of milled white rice?
quiz.explanation: White rice has about 7â8% protein, lower than brown rice because bran is removed.

quiz.q: Which vitamin is lost during milling of white rice?
quiz.explanation: B vitamins, especially B1 (thiamine), are concentrated in the bran and germ, which are removed.

quiz.q: What is the recommended roller clearance for milling long-grain rice?
quiz.explanation: Long-grain rice needs wider clearance (0.5â0.8 mm) to reduce cracking.

quiz.q: Which of these is a physical property of paddy?
quiz.explanation: Grain length is a physical property; amylose, protein, and aroma are chemical or sensory.

quiz.q: What does a moisture meter measure?
quiz.explanation: A moisture meter measures the percentage of water in the grain, critical for milling.

quiz.q: Which rice type is known for its aroma?
quiz.explanation: Basmati is a long-grain aromatic rice prized for its distinctive smell.

quiz.q: What is the typical head rice yield from paddy?
quiz.explanation: Good milling yields about 60â65% head rice, with the rest broken, bran, and husk.

quiz.q: Which factor increases breakage during milling?
quiz.explanation: Low moisture (below 12%) makes grains brittle and prone to shattering.

quiz.q: What is chalkiness in rice?
options: B) White opaque spots in the grain
quiz.explanation: Chalkiness refers to white opaque areas that weaken the grain and reduce milling yield.

quiz.q: Which of these is a step to improve grain grade?
quiz.explanation: Hand-picking removes discolored grains and foreign matter, improving grade.

quiz.q: What is the main carbohydrate in rice?
quiz.explanation: Starch makes up 75â80% of rice kernel dry weight.

quiz.q: Which rice subspecies is more common in African lowlands?
quiz.explanation: Indica rice dominates African lowland tropics due to its adaptation to warm climates.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a destoner in rice milling?
quiz.explanation: A destoner separates stones and other heavy foreign matter from paddy or milled rice.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a grade factor for milled rice?
quiz.explanation: Field yield is a production factor, not a grading criterion for milled rice.

quiz.q: What is the typical fat content of rice bran?
quiz.explanation: Rice bran contains about 10â15% fat, which can go rancid if not stabilized.

quiz.q: Which milling machine uses rubber rolls?
quiz.explanation: Rubber-roll huskers are gentler and cause less breakage than steel huskers.

quiz.q: What is the recommended storage condition for paddy?
quiz.explanation: Dry, ventilated storage keeps moisture stable and prevents mold and spoilage.

quiz.q: Which of these is a long-grain aromatic rice?
quiz.explanation: Jasmine is a long-grain aromatic rice, popular in Southeast Asia and Africa.

quiz.q: What does a 1000-grain weight indicate?
quiz.explanation: 1000-grain weight is a measure of grain size and density, affecting milling settings.
